thread.title: After The Fall: What Does Nvidia Do From Here? - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)

author: SA Marketplace
title: After The Fall: What Does Nvidia Do From Here? - NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)
text:
Seeking Alpha puts out a lot of ideas, and a lot of those ideas are well received by different audiences. A lot are not well received by different audiences. It's what makes a market and the nature of a crowdsourced platform. You can't please all the people all the time, especially when different people say different things. But the fun thing about the stock market is that the results matter, and ultimately, people's ideas are proven right or wrong (or at least, somewhat right or somewhat wrong).
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is a stock that has a lot of ideas on it, many of which are not well received and many of which are. The stock's precipitous rise over the past 3-4 years has attracted a lot of attention, as it gained ground with artificial intelligence chips and also caught a tailwind from crypto. After the rise came a fall, though, and the stock dropped as much as 50% this quarter. What happened?
Akram's Razor has been a long-time contributor on Seeking Alpha and never shy to enter a battleground. Author of The Razor's Edge on the SA Marketplace, He came to Nvidia afresh in February of this year and has stayed on the story regularly since then. The work he did exposed concerns in sell-side narratives and management's stories and drew on industry reports from around the world to unlock an opportunity in Nvidia shares, if from the short side.
After the stock sold off heavily in light of the company's lowering of guidance, SA Editor Daniel Shvartsman emailed with Akram about the Nvidia story to figure out what happened and what might come next for Nvidia and the companies in its sector.
What Happened To Nvidia Seeking Alpha: What did people get wrong about Nvidia?
Akram's Razor : Hah, just about everything. Daniel, as you know, in the summer of 2015, I got deep into a Mobileye ( MBLY ) ( INTC ) short thesis . Back before AI (artificial intelligence) was a market buzzword, Mobileye was the AI market pure play. You had Ron Baron on CNBC calling it the next WinTel and that they would own autonomous driving tech because of their superior machine learning algorithms.
Ironically, there was little old Nvidia trading at half the EV (enterprise value) of this name, literally a $7.5B EV and something close to 2x sales. This was with gaming, professional visualization biz, and of course, a just starting to form datacenter biz. I argued with NVDA vs. MBLY you got an already undervalued stock in two growing markets and a free option on AI, which the market wasn't recognizing. And while I did well on MBLY, which fell over 50% while I was short, the Nvidia long pair did over 5x.
Now, I moved on and did nothing with either name for all of 2017, but I had developed good knowledge and contacts in the ml/dl (machine learning/deep learning) space based on that work. Fast forward to early this year and crypto mania, and I started looking at Nvidia again from a pure crypto thesis. I learned that market pretty quick and concluding AMD ( AMD ) was being unfairly punished on crypto while Nvidia was sitting with much bigger exposure and not getting any heat for it.
But as I looked into Nvidia on crypto, I reignited my interest in what was going on in AI. And everything I found was classic semiconductor alarm bell stuff. Here was a $150-180bl company with almost 80% of its valuation locked up in belief that their GPUs (graphic processing units) would forever dominate ml/dl space. Yet, the poster child for AI, Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), was already on their third generation of an ml/dl chip. Then, as I learned about tensor cores, multiply accumulate, and the intricacies of what was going on in ml/dl inference vs. training etc., I was able to quickly see this was a once in a lifetime short.
The big super 7 hyperscalers were vertically integrating, and an avalanche of money was flowing into the chip startup space. I hadn't seen anything close to this since the comm IC (communication integrated circuits) mania of late '90s. Now, I have gotten to know a lot of the potential contenders in startup land, and some are very interesting. But picking a winner amongst 100 startups with all the hyperscalers doing what they are doing in-house and Intel/AMD and other large chip guys like Xilinx ( XLNX ) knocking on the door to me was virtually impossible. And then, you had the China element. They are approaching this space as they did with solar wafers, and they already had great success with ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits) in crypto mining, so that was another big concern.
Put it all together and picking a winner was impossible, but picking the only for sure loser was easy. No matter what happens, Nvidia loses market share and sees margins in datacenter come down. That's a nasty combination when you are paying 50x sales for a piece of the business which could end up being completely decimated at worst, or look far different than what the market expects at best. It was a no-brainer. Add in its darling reputation and the fact that nobody else was doing this work on it, and well, you had the ultimate mega-cap asymmetric bet. And remember, I paired this off with Google at $995 and Broadcom ( AVGO ) at $220 at the time just to hedge out Nasdaq mania risk. Look where those two names are after the tech wreck, both are green. From my standpoint, that's almost as impressive as the fact that Nvidia collapsed as well.
SA: You've called management promotional here and suggest they have lost credibility. You've been bullish on Nvidia in past years, so when do you feel management became an issue, and what happened?
AR: Jensen is a classic founder CEO. He's obviously super-passionate about the company he's built, and he should be as he's built a great one. But you could see him losing the plot a bit earlier in the year. For me, the first big red flag was on the Feb q4 call when he started attributing everything going right in Gaming GPU to PUBG and Fortnite. And then, it got worse on the Q1 call which came after crypto's first big crash. One analyst asked about how gaming revenue was up sequentially, and he literally summed it up with "the simple answer to your question is Fortnite and PUBG. And, the demand is just really great. They did a great job."
This to me was a very reckless response. Here, I was looking at these numbers and scratching my head. How the heck was gaming growing sequentially after this crypto craziness had started, and how where they guiding the way they were. It made zero sense. There literally was only one explanation, and that was that Nvidia's ASPs (average sales prices) on GPUs had drastically risen. Think about the Apple ( AAPL ) debate because it's a perfect analogy. Apple has killed it on iPhone ASPs as units have been flat. They have done this by leveraging their scale as a DRAM buyer and upping the memory in the phones.
Now Apple, until they said they would no longer do this on their last call, breaks out ASPs and Units. Nvidia provides neither. Here, we had the greatest bubble since Tulip mania, and the number one supplier to the space is not grilled on their ASPs. We could see the madness in the AIB numbers, and even DigiTimes reported in late February that Nvidia had taken a big price increase on the channel to offset for unit declines. Well, how big? Not a single one of the 30 analysts covering the name bothered asking this question. Of course, I finally got my answer when PC Partner, which sells exclusive Nvidia branded Graphics Cards under the Zotac brand name, disclosed this info in early October. Their branded gaming card biz for the first six months of 2018 was up 76% over 2017. How much was ASP? All of it!! Yes, unit shipments were flat. They sold the same amount of gaming cards in h1 2018 as they did in h1 2017. Now, this is common sense stuff. Crediting PUBG/Fortnite for 50%+ yr/yr revenue growth is nonsensical. The gaming PC market didn't grow that much or else we'd have seen it in other places. But completely flat, which is what I had expected btw, was the ultimate confirmation. And here was this data being disclosed by a public company, and nobody was looking at it. Suffice to say that's a nice edge to have on a $150bl company.
And there was so much more out of Nvidia mgmt. The Uber/Tesla ( UBER ) ( TSLA ) stuff on autonomous driving, for example. They announce these companies have adopted their tech, and then when something goes wrong, you get a different explanation. In Uber's case, it was they using offshelf GPUs, not the whole platform. Well, then what was the PR about earlier where you characterized them differently. And Tesla going to their own chip after you saying Tesla was 5 years ahead of everyone because of your chip? Or how about Jensen saying not to expect new cards for a 'long time'. The rumors of returns and Nvidia pressuring AIBs to take Pascal cards or risk lower Turing allocations. It was red flag central.
As far as I am concerned, management knew full well crypto drove gaming massively and just figured they could navigate it. Why? Well, if you disclosed massive ASP driven gains driving gaming revenue the market would discount that immediately to crypto. Their plan was very simple. As soon as crypto crashes, we come out with Turing at these much higher ASPs. Gamers will gobble them up, and we never miss a beat quarter and maintain higher ASPs going forward. They gambled big and got it wrong. Then they come out after and say well crypto surprised us. In that case, please go ahead and disclose units vs ASPs before Turing launch because that is not what you were saying a few months ago. Where did all the PUBG/Fortnite talk go?
SA: What did you hear from the sell-side in response to your work, especially given you challenged them frequently?
AR: The sell-side was a mess on this name. I've never seen it so bad on such a big company. I sat in on several calls with many of these guys, and every time my jaw would drop. Their biggest issue was the AI Ml/DL stuff. I mean utterly clueless across the board on the space. Just regurgitating Nvidia's narrative. I mean think about this for a second. Google is literally out there showing off its TPUs (tensor processing units), and it is the world's leading AI company. They stick them in Google Cloud right next to Nvidia's GPUs, and their pitch is we have everything for you here, but our TPUs are faster and cheaper if you want to try them.
Meanwhile, all the sell-side tells you is Google Cloud has adopted Volta, yay. Well, guys maybe take a closer look. Google's GCP sales associates are out there saying you can use GPUs on AWS or Azure and we have them too, but what these guys don't have is these amazing TPUs. Want to leverage them? You can only do that on GCP. And then eBay ( EBAY ), which has an in-house Nvidia-based training cluster, comes out and literally provides a blog post saying we moved to Google Cloud TPUs. And they tell you why. Faster, cheaper, and we avoid capex for chips that may be obsolete in a very short-time considering the pace of development in the space.
Maybe you may want to mention that in a report? Nope. Instead they were doing the opposite. I kid you not, there was one analyst out there that said Google would be a 10% customer for Nvidia this year when they filed their 10-k. Think about that for a second. That means at least $1.3 billion in Nvidia revenue from Google. Is every Google employee playing Fortnite? I mean that would be half of Datacenter coming from Google. Is the TPU just a fun side project despite it providing all acceleration for Google's production-neural nets? Like it made no sense.
Then, in my one article , I highlighted the Goldman Sachs note which said to buy Nvidia post Turing launch. The analyst literally put a table together and took Nvidia's claims on Turing performance being 6x and applied it to AI ML/DL performance. The table has Google's TPUs looking like Minnie Mouse next to 1000+ Teraflop DL performance from Turing. Of course, that's not the case. Turing is actually not even as powerful as Volta for training, and it's not supposed to be. The 6x claim was for certain ray tracing elements in gaming vs. Pascal. So, Goldman can't understand the difference between Gaming and Datacenter? Because nobody with even half decent understanding of ML/DL would put a table like that together. But what can you say, you raise some polite questions, and then few days later, the stock is added to focus list or whatever. That's just the business. These guys with all they do just don't have the time to dive into a new space like this and really grasp it. So, they assume someone else has or else they'd have heard something already if they were so wrong.
It's groupthink at its worst. I mean it's funny that yesterday AWS announced their AI chip for datacenter inference. Now, I've been saying for months AWS, which by the way is Nvidia's biggest AI datacenter customer, will follow Google and everyone else building chips. It's literally what Amazon does for a living. And not a single note cautioning on this, but 20 saying buy Nvidia into earnings because the T4 Inferencing card will be available in major clouds. And the best part is go to AWS press release on this. They explicitly say they have done this because 'GPUs are too expensive for scale out inferencing'... hint Nvidia datacenter margins!
What Comes Next SA: Citron Research recently flipped to long NVDA. What do you think about that?
AR: I know Citron. I think you have to distinguish between when Andrew makes a trading call and when he makes a fundamental call. He's got excellent trader instincts, and I also am active as a trader. I think it was a brilliant call by him. Timing wise, it was impeccable. I mean the stock printed 133 on the open when he put that out. Personally, I went long some Facebook ( FB ) and Salesforce ( CRM ) there as that low volume gap down hit everything. Could I have bought Nvidia for a trade? Yeah, it was clearly getting mass liquidated, but risk wise, I was more comfy elsewhere. But he was right... Nvidia was more likely to see 165 before it sees 120. He didn't say buy and hold this forever again. So, kudos to him. How much of the bounce was anything fundamental in Nvidia vs. the market? I'd say zero, but he found the name most likely to snap back hardest which is what excellent traders do. Everything in that battered tech category got at least 10% from Tuesday, except my Facebook position naturally. But I'm happy with Salesforce, and long either of these for a trade I sleep better at night.
SA: You have been flexible with your positioning on stocks as stories change, as with Veeva ( VEEV ). What would you need to see from Nvidia to change the story?
AR: Nvidia now has this Gaming headache tied to an inventory correction. Nobody is out there saying start worrying about datacenter, which is what I find interesting. The stock didn't shed 90 billion because of gaming. Best case scenario, Nvidia, ex AI, is a 40-50bl company. The real story with the name lately has been datacenter slowing, and that's still not frontpage news. I think the problem longs have here is just about the time gaming is normalizing, all anyone is going to be talking about is AI chip competitors and how that biz is changing.
Remember you got Graphcore telling you their whole 1st production run is sold out. Huawei with an offering. Bitmain winning some video acceleration biz in Asia. AMD talking up some progress. 10 other startups showing off chips that are blowing Nvidia performance away. Tesla moving to their own chip which by the way you should see show up in their auto revenue soon. Google ramping up their TPU cloud. XLNX's AI chip. Intel's chip launching this year. And on and on... you want to be long into that news flow and dynamics? I don't.
Now, what could change my mind. Simple, all these competitors gradually failing, but how long till we can measure that clearly? It's going to take time. So, I'd need the stock at a price where I get the rest of Nvidia's biz at a good value and Datacenter optionality again. I think that's more balanced around $100. But I doubt it gets there anytime soon. The name probably trades between 140 and 170 for now.
SA: Given that range and outlook, what are you doing with Nvidia now in your portfolio, and why?
AR: Right now, I have no position as I think the easy asymmetric money has been made, and it's going to take time for market to digest the datacenter debate as everyone hung up on crypto. But as I wrote in last article, I view it as uninvestable for now. Meaning you can't buy and hold it at these levels with any degree of confidence. The shifting landscape and increasing competitive environment in ml/dl is still the elephant in the room as far as sell-side goes, and the news flow there isn't shifting to Nvidia's favor anytime soon. Why would you want the headache of press releases like AWS yesterday which are not going to cease anytime soon? The point that changes for me would be about 30% lower.
SA: What should investors learn from this story?
AR: Do your homework. Assumption is the mother of all...
Other Stocks To Watch SA: You have been long at times this year on AMD. Current outlook for that company?
AR: I have no view. I'd been long AMD from 3 to 10 and again from like 11 to 17. Missed the madness to 35, but whatever. I don't think AMD will be a player in GPU Datacenter AI as many hope. It doesn't fit with my thesis. It's been a nice trade on CPU side vs Intel, and I think Lisa has done amazing job of communicating to market more clearly on crypto and GPU biz. But if you think GPUs are going to hold their ground in ML/DL, get long Nvidia.
I do think though in gaming AMD now has an opportunity as Nvidia has stumbled with Turing. Gamers like myself are happily waiting for them to give us something as we are kind of a little tired of way Nvidia has been going dominating the market as it has. Wouldn't take much out of AMD to get me to switch. But, overall, if you think big picture, Intel/AMD/Nvidia all face risks here as the vertical integration by cloud giants and huge explosion in specialty purpose chips for certain workloads will long-term pressure their margins. A place I had liked in chips was the companies benefiting from a huge investment cycle in semi-startups. Every startup needs to do biz with Cadence ( CDNS ) or Synopsys ( SNPS ), and they all need to tape out at Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ). But I've sold all my cadence here as it's done so well.
SA: What's another idea you are following, and what's the story?
AR: I have been looking at Nutanix ( NTNX ) closely. I really like the story there despite the valuation. I don't see how the name stays independent. I'll probably share my views in a report at some point, so let's leave it at that. I like Salesforce.com a lot, to me the cheapest name in software. I actually don't like Veeva again, but again, I'll probably share views on that somewhere down the road.
The bottom line with this market right now is it's been so macro-driven, so very tough to get into individual stories when there is so much trading to do. I've dabbled long Alibaba ( BABA ) and Tencent ( OTCPK:TCEHY ) as the China tech went first, so figured better place to go shopping. And I love Facebook here as way too much is priced into it. Google and Broadcom have been great but I'm out of both as they outperformed too much. I love Google the most of all the names if you are a buy and hold conservative type, but right now, there are better deals elsewhere.
